title: Data Lakes
summary: A lake stores raw data cheaply before deciding how to model it, trading a warehouse's guarantees and structure for flexibility and cost — a trade that only pays off with real lineage and ownership discipline behind it.

slides.markdown:
A [warehouse](warehouse-fundamentals) makes you decide a schema before you load data. A **data lake** lets you dump raw data first — logs, JSON blobs, images, whatever a source system produces — and decide how to model it later, or never, if it turns out you don't need to.

That flexibility is genuinely valuable, and it comes with a real cost: without deliberate structure and process, a lake degrades into a **data swamp** — a pile of files nobody can reliably use. This topic covers what a lake actually is architecturally, the schema-on-read trade-off that defines it, and the discipline required to keep it useful.

A data lake's foundation is **object storage** — a flat, massively scalable store of files ("objects"), each identified by a key, with no built-in notion of rows, columns, or schema. Object storage is cheap (often a fraction of the cost per gigabyte of a database's storage), extremely durable, and scales to effectively unlimited size without needing you to provision anything in advance.

Crucially, object storage doesn't care what's inside a file — a CSV, a JSON blob, an image, a Parquet file, a raw log line — it's just bytes under a key. That schema-less-ness is the entire basis for the lake's flexibility: you can write data the moment you have it, in whatever shape the source produces, without a schema design step blocking ingestion.

The trade-off is that object storage alone gives you nowhere to enforce structure, consistency, or query performance — every one of those has to be built as a layer on top, which is exactly what the rest of this group (and Lakehouse Table Formats specifically) is about.

A warehouse enforces **schema-on-write**: you define column names and types before loading data, and every write has to conform. A lake defaults to **schema-on-read**: data is written as-is, in whatever shape it arrived, and the schema is only interpreted — inferred, or applied by whatever job reads it — at query time.

This inversion is the direct cause of both the lake's flexibility and its risk. Flexibility: you can ingest data from a source before anyone has designed how it should be modeled, and different consumers can interpret the same raw files differently for different purposes. Risk: nothing stops the underlying data from silently changing shape between writes — a source system adds a field, renames one, or changes a type — and you only discover it when a downstream read job breaks or, worse, silently produces wrong results.

Schema-on-read isn't free-form chaos by necessity — it's a deferred decision, and how well that defers versus simply postpones a problem depends entirely on whether anyone is tracking what shape the data is actually in.

A common way to bring order to a lake without abandoning its flexibility is a **layered zone structure**: raw/**bronze** data lands exactly as ingested, unmodified — a permanent, replayable record of the source. **Silver** holds data that's been cleaned, deduplicated, and lightly conformed to a consistent schema. **Gold** holds curated, business-ready datasets — aggregated, joined, and modeled for a specific consumption purpose, often the layer that actually feeds dashboards or a warehouse.

slides.subTitle: Cost, flexibility, performance, governance
slides.markdown:
| | Data lake | Data warehouse |
|---|---|---|
| Storage cost | Lower — plain object storage | Higher — often bundled with compute or a managed storage layer |
| Schema flexibility | High — schema-on-read, any file format | Lower — schema-on-write, structured tables |
| Query performance (out of the box) | Lower — no built-in columnar/MPP optimizations | Higher — purpose-built for fast aggregation |
| Governance and ACID guarantees | Historically weak, without an added table-format layer | Strong — transactions, constraints, established tooling |

Neither column is strictly better — a lake wins on cost and flexibility for raw and semi-structured data at scale; a warehouse wins on query performance and governance for curated, structured analytics. Many real architectures use both: a lake for raw and intermediate zones, a warehouse (or a lakehouse table format, covered next) for the curated layer that actually serves fast, governed queries.

A lake with no lineage tracking, no clear ownership per dataset, and no quality checks degrades over time into a **data swamp** — a large, cheap pile of files that nobody trusts and few people can navigate. Symptoms accumulate quietly: duplicate datasets with slightly different names and unclear which is current, files whose schema silently drifted with no record of when or why, and no way to trace a downstream number back to which raw source produced it.

The swamp doesn't happen from one bad decision — it accumulates from many small ones: skipping documentation "just this once," landing a one-off export with no owner assigned, not enforcing any naming or zone convention because the deadline was tight. Each is individually reasonable; the accumulated effect is a lake where finding trustworthy data takes longer than it would have taken to just re-derive it from the source.

The fix is process, not tooling alone: assigned ownership per dataset, a documented zone convention (bronze/silver/gold or equivalent) that's actually enforced, and lineage tracking so any dataset's origin and transformations are traceable.

slides.sectionTitle: Why lakes historically lacked ACID guarantees
slides.markdown:
Object storage was designed for durably storing and retrieving whole files, not for the fine-grained, multi-file, transactional updates a database takes for granted. Writing a "table" as a directory of files on object storage means an update that touches multiple files has no native way to make all those changes appear atomically — a reader could see some files updated and others not, mid-write, with nothing preventing it.

This mattered concretely: a job overwriting a dataset that fails halfway through could leave the lake in an inconsistent state — some files reflecting the new data, some the old — and concurrent writers had no built-in mechanism to avoid stepping on each other's changes.

This gap is precisely what the next-but-one topic, Lakehouse Table Formats, exists to close: an added metadata layer on top of plain files that brings warehouse-grade ACID guarantees, schema enforcement, and time travel directly to lake storage, without giving up the lake's underlying cost and flexibility advantages.

slides.sectionTitle: What a lake is good at that a warehouse isn't
slides.markdown:
A lake's schema-less flexibility isn't just a workaround for lacking structure — it's genuinely the right tool for some workloads a warehouse handles poorly or not at all:

- **Unstructured and semi-structured data** — images, audio, free-text documents, nested JSON with varying shape — a warehouse's table model doesn't fit this data well, while a lake stores it natively as files with no forced structure.
- **ML training data** — machine learning pipelines commonly need raw, high-volume data (images, feature-rich event logs) in flexible formats that training frameworks read directly, not necessarily pre-aggregated into warehouse tables.
- **Cheap long-term retention of raw history** — keeping years of raw source data "just in case" is far more affordable in object storage than in a warehouse's storage tier, making a lake the natural place to retain the deep history a Kappa-style replay (from the Stream Processing group) or a future reprocessing need might require.

The practical pattern: raw and less-structured data lives in the lake; the curated, aggregation-ready subset that actually needs fast structured queries gets promoted into a warehouse or a lakehouse table format.

To make the cost trade-off concrete: cloud object storage commonly runs on the order of a couple of cents per GB per month for standard-tier storage, with cheaper archival tiers available for data accessed rarely. A comparably-sized warehouse-managed storage tier, when it's not simply built on the same underlying object storage, can cost noticeably more per GB, especially when it's bundled with compute capacity you're not fully utilizing.

At a petabyte of raw retained history, that difference is the gap between a storage bill in the low thousands of dollars per month and one that can run several times higher depending on the platform and tier — which is exactly why "keep everything in the lake, promote only what's needed into the warehouse" is the dominant cost-conscious pattern rather than loading everything into warehouse-managed storage by default.

These are illustrative figures, not quotes — actual pricing varies by provider, region, and access pattern — but the order-of-magnitude gap is real and is the concrete reason lakes remain the default landing zone for raw data even at organizations with a mature warehouse.

This topic covered the lake as it was originally conceived — cheap, flexible, and lacking a warehouse's transactional guarantees. That last gap is exactly what the next topic, Lakehouse Table Formats, closes: adding a metadata layer on top of the same plain files that brings ACID transactions, schema enforcement, and time travel to lake storage, blurring the once-sharp line between "lake" and "warehouse" that this topic's comparison table drew.

The zone pattern (bronze/silver/gold) and the swamp risk covered here don't go away with a lakehouse format layered on top — they're still the operational discipline a lakehouse needs, just with stronger guarantees available at the storage layer underneath.
